13.0.0.en: "A wise son heareth his father's instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke." [1]

13.0.1.en: It is fitting for parents to represent the Fatherhood of God and the motherhood of the holy Church, declaring to the child from his birth true and wise love, so that the child grows up in a joyful, heavenly atmosphere and bows in a spirit of obedience, to draw from the wisdom in which his parents live in the Lord. Thus the son, in the spirit of wisdom, accepts the conduct of his parents, full of love even in their firmness and in their discipline of him.

13.0.2.en: The wise son, in a spirit of need and gratitude, seeks wisdom and help; but the son who does not listen to his parents, in scorn and heedlessness, loses the blessings of wisdom. He walks in arrogance, making light of others, refusing discipline and reproof. In a spirit of self-importance he despises the words of the wise.

13.0.3.en: * My children, everyone who hears discipline and does not accept it or act on it is losing his own soul, and becomes constantly tormented in soul; his mind is never at rest, and he becomes irritable, sad, gloomy, anxious, grieved and full of thoughts; his soul demands of him to do evil and to speak foul words. For discipline is like the king's highway, on which guards keep watch day and night, so that everyone who walks on it by day or by night is safe! But ignorance, deafness and self-admiration are a rough road that is not traveled, and everyone who walks in it goes astray and grows weary and perhaps perishes, for the haunt of robbers is there! And everyone who walked on the traveled road and happened to stumble in some matter or accident, his excuse was spread out and his remedy at hand; but he who left the king's highway and chose to walk on the rough road has neither excuse nor remedy.

13.1.0.en: 2 A man eats good from the fruit of his mouth, and the desire of the treacherous is wrong. 3 He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction. 4 The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat. 5 The righteous hates false speech, and the wicked brings shame and disgrace.

13.1.1.en: The Lord Christ says: "A good man out of the good treasure bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things. But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:35-37).

13.1.2.en: "A man eats good from the fruit of his mouth, and the desire of the treacherous is wrong." [2]

13.1.3.en: The wise man desires good for all, so his words come from between his lips full of sweetness and tenderness; he eats of them and his soul rejoices. But the wicked man's heart gives forth treachery and deceit, which his words express; he eats of them and his soul hungers all the more for violence and wrong.

13.1.4.en: In other words, as a man offers his words to others, they become food for him. If he offers his words anointed with grace, he enjoys grace within him; and if he offers evil words, they return to him.

13.1.5.en: * My son... let your heart be humble, and your mouth always speak the truth.

13.1.6.en: * Do not slander anyone, lest God hate your prayer. Beware of play and mockery, for it drives the fear of God out of the heart.

13.1.7.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great * Teach your mouth to say what is in your heart.

13.2.0.en: St. Abba Poemen "He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction." [3]

13.2.1.en: He who guards his mouth guards his life. The spiritually mature man controls his tongue for his edification, and the foolish man destroys himself with his words.

13.2.2.en: Some see in opening the lips wide, or exaggeratedly, a reference to a man's speaking in a crooked way, where the words carry two meanings, the apparent meaning concealing a hidden meaning that destroys the soul.

13.2.3.en: And some see that opening the lips wide means not being bound by any set limits for the words one utters, but speaking about everything, at any time and without limit, without balanced thought before speaking.

13.2.4.en: God gave man two eyes so that he might see, examine and observe closely, and also two ears so that he might hear and listen with long-suffering, but He gave him one tongue so that he might be guarded and brief in his words, especially as the tongue is surrounded by barriers, the lips and the teeth.

13.2.5.en: * Let your speech be sweet and without loss, for glory and shame come from speech. Love mercy and arm yourself with faith.

13.2.6.en: * My son, do not make your heart wicked so that it thinks evil, but make it good, and seek goodness and acquire zeal in all good works. Do not raise your voice, and if you go to someone, let the fear of God be in your heart, and guard your mouth that you may return to your place in peace. Do not multiply words before one who is older than you.

13.3.0.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat." [4]

13.3.1.en: In spiritual matters as in bodily matters, "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10). He who diligently seeks the truth in the word of God rejoices in the word like one who finds spoil. As the psalmist says: "I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil" (Ps 119:162).

13.3.2.en: It is fitting for us to work diligently: "Consider your ways" (Hag 1:6).

13.3.3.en: "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men (Prov 22:29).

13.3.4.en: "Strive to enter in at the strait gate" (Lk 13:24).

13.3.5.en: "Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall" (2 Pet 1:10).

13.3.6.en: "Be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless" (2 Pet 3:14).

13.3.7.en: "I write unto you, exhorting you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (Jude 1:3).

13.3.8.en: * My son... think on the works of God and do not be lazy, for the prayer of the lazy is vain speech. Strive to keep away from men who lack counsel. If you do virtuous deeds, do not boast and say, I have done them. For if you think that you have done them, you are not wise. It is a shame for you to command others with commands you have not carried out in yourself, for you do not profit from another's work. The wise man knows the way of his conduct, so he does not hasten to speak, but considers what he says and what he does.

13.3.9.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great * Thus I see you both fallen under this weakness of laziness which the Book of Proverbs describes: "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing," and also "The desire of the slothful killeth him" (Prov 13:4; 21:25). For it is not fitting for us to be at ease concerning our temporal needs so long as these needs are necessary and proportionate to our calling. If we think that we can acquire for ourselves great gain from those delights that spring from bodily feelings, shall we not strip from ourselves the consolation of our relatives? Does the saying of our Savior not restrain us, which removes us from all that is attributed to the needs of the body, saying: "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters... he cannot be my disciple" (Lk 14:26)?

13.3.10.en: Abba Abraham * Solomon, the wisest of men, points to this vice in many of his writings when he says: "He that followeth after vain persons shall have poverty enough" (Prov 28:19), either openly or in secret, for the slack man cannot but become entangled. And whoever is pursued by shortcomings never discerns the divine contemplations or the spiritual treasures, to which the blessed Apostle points when he says: "That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge" (1 Cor 1:5).

13.3.11.en: As for this poverty that befalls the lazy man, that is, the weary one, he also writes: "The sluggard shall be clothed with rags" (Prov 23:21). Surely he does not deserve to be adorned with that garment which no misfortune or corruption will touch, of which the Apostle says: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14), and also: "Putting on the breastplate of faith and love" (1 Thess 5:8), and of which the Lord Himself spoke to Jerusalem by the mouth of the prophet, saying: "Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion" (Isa 51:1).

13.3.12.en: Anyone overcome by the sleep of slackness or weariness prefers to be clothed not with his work and toil, but with the rags of laziness, quoting (and misusing) phrases from the firm Holy Scripture, without clothing his laziness in a garment of glory and honor, but in a robe of shame and the seeking of excuses. Those are the ones who prefer this laziness and do not wish to support themselves by the labor of their hands, as the Apostle always did and charged us to do, saying that it is written: "Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life" (Jn 6:27), and also: "My meat is to do the will of my Father" (Jn 4:34). But these proofs are rags torn from the firm and solid garment of the Gospel, taken for this purpose, I mean to cover the scandal of our laziness and our shame, instead of providing us with warmth and our being adorned with the splendid and costly garment of virtue; for it is said that the woman mentioned in the Book of Proverbs, who was wrapped in strength and splendor, made garments either for herself or for her husband, so that it is said of her at all times: "Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come" (Prov 31:25).

13.3.13.en: Solomon returns once more to mention the plague of laziness, saying: "The way of the sluggard is strewn with thorns" (Prov 15:29), that is, strewn with these and other similar defects which the Apostle said earlier spring from idleness. Likewise he says: "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing" (Prov 13:4), and the Apostle points to this desiring when he says: "And that ye may have need of no man" (1 Thess 4:12). Finally the Apostle enumerated those plagues which the wise Solomon said are the planting of idleness and weariness, in the passage just mentioned, by saying: "Working not at all, but are busybodies" (1 Thess 4:11). And he adds to this plague another, saying: "And that ye study to be quiet," then "to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, and to walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have need of no man" (1 Thess 4:11).

13.3.14.en: As for those who walk disorderly and do not obey the commandments, the Apostle charges the earnest children of obedience to withdraw from them, saying: "Withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us" (2 Thess 3:6).

13.4.0.en: St. John Cassian "A righteous man hateth lying: but the wicked brings shame and disgrace." [5]

13.4.1.en: The heart committed to the truth becomes a source of practical righteousness in Christ Jesus. It becomes a throne for the Holy One, and hates vain abominations and lying. It finds its happiness in fellowship with God and in glorifying His holy name in the midst of this wicked world that resists the truth. But the wicked man corrupts his depths by his sin, to carry within him the smell of death and stench. He becomes naked in this world, and is cast into outer darkness on the great day of the Lord.

13.4.2.en: The man of God not only avoids lying, but hates it and cannot bear it.

13.4.3.en: Beware of lying, for it drives the fear of God out of a man.

13.4.4.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great * Let us refuse the honor and dignities of the world that we may be rid of vainglory, and let us use the tongue in remembering God and the truth that we may be rid of lying.

13.5.0.en: 6 Righteousness keepeth him that is upright in the way: but wickedness overthroweth the sinner. 7 There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches. 8 The ransom of a man's life are his riches: but the poor heareth not rebuke.

13.5.1.en: "Righteousness keepeth him that is upright in the way: but wickedness overthroweth the sinner." [6]

13.5.2.en: Whoever earnestly desires to walk uprightly in the righteousness of Christ, righteousness keeps him from grave errors, keeps him perfect in the eyes of God, that he may receive fellowship in eternal glory. But as for him who is set on evil, his destruction comes to him from within, from evil, the giver of corruption.

13.6.0.en: "There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches." [7]

13.6.1.en: Some pretend to be rich while inwardly they are poor. This is the sin of vainglory and the love of greatness with hypocrisy. Yet there are those who are rich in their depths, overflowing with good things, and in humility consider themselves poor, in need of God's continual grace and the prayers of others. The rich Apostle Paul says: "As poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" (2 Cor 10:6), while the Lord rebukes the angel of the church of the Laodiceans, saying: "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked" (Rev 3:16-17).

13.6.2.en: This is the work of the nature of the old man which we inherited from our father Adam: with our inner poverty we pretend to be rich!

13.6.3.en: * The sickness of the rich man is dangerous pride.

13.6.4.en: The truly great spirit in the midst of wealth does not prostrate itself and fall into this sickness.

13.6.5.en: The spirit is greater than its wealth and rises above it, not by desiring it, but by despising it.

13.6.6.en: Truly great is that rich man who does not think himself great because of his wealth. But if he considers himself great, he is thereby proud and destitute...! He is a beggar in his (empty) heart. He is puffed up and not full.

13.6.7.en: If you see two wineskins, one full and the other inflated, they have the same size and the same extent, but they do not have the same contents. Look at them and you cannot tell them apart; weigh them and you will find the difference between them. The full wineskin is hard to move, and the inflated one can be moved easily...

13.6.8.en: I am not telling you to squander your wealth but to transfer it, for there are many who refused to do this and, alas, did not obey; they lost not only their wealth, but because of it they also lost their souls...

13.6.9.en: Let (the rich man) be humble. Let him be glad that he is a Christian rather than that he is rich. Let him not be puffed up or exalted or overbearing. Let him care for his poor brother, and not refuse to call the poor man his brother. Above all this, however great his wealth, Christ is richer still, and He wished all those for whom He shed His blood to be His brothers.

13.7.0.en: St. Augustine "The ransom of a man's life are his riches: but the poor heareth not rebuke." [8]

13.7.1.en: Some interpret this phrase to mean that wealth often causes the loss of happiness, so that some rich men are exposed to kidnapping, or their children are kidnapped, in the hope of gaining a share of their money as a ransom for them; but as for the poor man, no one thinks of kidnapping him!

13.7.2.en: Here he speaks of the rich man who sets his whole heart on his money, so that he becomes a captive to his possessions; they possess him and he does not possess them, so he lives in anxiety and agitation. He also speaks of the pious poor man who, in complete surrender, takes no thought for the morrow, that is, his soul is neither troubled nor anxious. Yet we do not deny that some rich men who put their trust in God, like Abraham the father of fathers, who was very, very rich according to the testimony of the Holy Bible, lived a blessed life, happy in God. And there are poor men who possess nothing and live in anxiety, because they have not put their hearts in the hand of God.

13.7.3.en: Origen says that those who misuse their wealth sin. And many of the poor share the same punishment, who, while suffering from poverty, behave in a base and mean manner. Even those who are in a middle state, between the rich and the poor, this state does not mean that it keeps them from falling into sin.

13.7.4.en: A person's wealth must work for the salvation of his soul, not for its destruction. Wealth is the redemption of him who uses it well. Wealth is a snare for him who does not know how to use it. For what is a man's money unless it supports him on his journey? A large amount of it is a burden, and a little of it is useful. We are travelers in this life; many walk together, but a person needs to walk a good road. The Lord Jesus is with him who walks the good road.

13.7.5.en: * The rich man is not blamed in himself, for "the ransom of a man's life are his riches," since by giving to the poor he saves his soul. For there is a place for virtue even in material wealth. You are like helmsmen in the midst of a wide sea. If a man steers rightly he passes quickly over the sea and reaches the harbor. But he who does not know how to steer his possessions sinks with his cargo. For the wealth of the rich is a very strong city.

13.7.6.en: St. Ambrose * In this sense, "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate" (1 Tim 6:17-18). And as Solomon says: the truly good "riches" are "the ransom of a man's life," while the poverty opposed to this wealth is destructive, for by it "the poor cannot hear rebuke."

13.7.7.en: Origen * "The ransom of a man's life are his riches." What are you saying? What do you mean by glorifying such wealth? First of all (Solomon) does not speak of just any wealth, but of the wealth that is gained through honorable deeds. Therefore poverty is not an evil. He says: rather, no one is able to threaten a poor man; indeed, how can anyone terrify one who has nothing? Therefore such a life avoids sorrows.

13.7.8.en: Perhaps (Solomon) here calls "his riches" "his righteousness," which snatches him from death. For he who is poor in virtue has no peace of mind when he suffers threats and the announcement of punishment.

13.7.9.en: * Paul says: "Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do" (Gal 2:10). We find much concerning this matter everywhere in the Holy Bible. It is said: "The ransom of a man's life are his riches"... And (Christ) says: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor... and come and follow me" (Mt 19:21). This is part of perfection.

13.7.10.en: St. John Chrysostom * Scripture affirms that true riches are the ransom of a man, meaning that if he is rich he is saved by distributing his wealth. For just as, when water is drawn from wells, their flow returns to the first level, so giving is a spring of useful love; by offering its water to the thirsty it increases and is filled again, just as milk is wont to flow from the breast when it is suckled or milked.

13.7.11.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * The Lord yearns for the souls of believers more than for their wealth. We read in Proverbs: "The ransom of a man's life are his riches." In truth we may regard a man's wealth as that wealth which does not come from another person or from plunder, according to the commandment: "Honour the Lord with your righteous labors" (cf. Prov 3:9). The meaning becomes better if we understand a person's wealth to be the hidden treasures which no thief can steal and no robber can seize from him (cf. Mt 6:20).

13.7.12.en: St. Jerome * Good wealth (possessions) is what the acquirer of virtues possesses... the doer of righteousness whom the prophet David praises, saying: "His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed. Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever" (Ps 112:2-3). And also "The ransom of a man's life are his riches" (Prov 13:8). And the Book of Revelation speaks to the one lacking and destitute of this wealth, saying: "I will spue thee out of my mouth. Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked: I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear" (Rev 3:16-18).

13.7.13.en: Abba Paphnutius * Suppose you are a person of lowly birth and no distinction, poor, of a low class, without house or city, sick, in need of daily bread, fearing those in authority, trembling before everyone because of your circumstances; the Holy Bible says: "But the poor heareth not rebuke" (Prov 13:8). Yes, do not despair or lose all good hope, because your present state is by no means to be envied. Rather turn your thoughts to the blessings you have already received from God, and the blessings reserved for you by the special promise of the future.

13.8.0.en: "The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out." [9]

13.8.1.en: What is the light of the righteous but the Holy Spirit of God, the giver of illumination? He shines upon the righteous and gives them His fruit, that is, joy, as the Spirit rejoices in them. The Lord Christ says: "I am the light of the world"; as He shines upon those who believe in Him, He rejoices in them as in a radiant bride bearing the reflection of His splendor, and they themselves become the light of the world.

13.8.2.en: As for the lamp of the wicked, it is the light of their own knowledge, which, though it shines for moments, is quickly put out.

13.8.3.en: Some see that the light and the lamp here are the offspring of a man; the righteous, caring for the salvation of their sons, have their sons filled with joy, and the children even become a source of joy to their parents and to those around them. But the offspring of the wicked seem to prosper, yet their light is soon put out.

13.8.4.en: It is said of King Abijam: "Nevertheless for David's sake did the LORD his God give him a lamp in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him, and to establish Jerusalem" (1 Kgs 15:4). It is also said: "And unto his son will I give one tribe, that David my servant may have a lamp alway before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen me to put my name there" (1 Kgs 11:36).

13.8.5.en: In the parable of the ten virgins (Mt 25:1-13), the lamps of the wise virgins were burning, and remain burning forever through the oil of God's surpassing grace working in them with love, but the foolish virgins could not light their lamps because they carried no oil.

13.8.6.en: * Children who are obedient and faithful to God in their obedience to His law find a source overflowing with happiness even in this temporal life. A poor man with Christian morals inspires others to show him reverence and love. But he who has a wicked and perverse heart, all his wealth will not save him from the anger of all around him and their hatred of him.

13.9.s.en: 5. The spirit of wisdom and agreement

13.9.0.en: "Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom." [10]

13.9.1.en: Quarrels between individuals, families or nations arise because of pride. For this reason the Lord Christ gave us salvation by coming down to us in wonderful humility, and accepting the shame of the Cross to reconcile us with the Father, as with the heavenly beings, and with one another.

13.9.2.en: When a strife arose between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle, Abram, with a spirit of dialogue full of humility, was able to put an end to the strife, saying to his nephew: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren. Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left" (Gen 13:8-9).

13.9.3.en: * The man of strife who does not rest from conflict is the one who is not content with the first quarrel, and so rises in anger again. But he who is not a man of strife, when his anger is kindled, returns to himself at once, and blames himself, and asks forgiveness of his brother with whom he was angry, so the strife in him is quieted because he has condemned himself and been reconciled with his brother, and conflict will find no place in him, as I said.

13.9.4.en: But the wrathful man, in whom the discord does not subside, who when he is angry does not condemn himself, but his anger rises all the more without his ever repenting of his anger, and who is not even content with what he said in his anger but adds to it; this one is called a man of strife, and the anger does not subside within him, because grudge, bitterness and malice follow anger. May the Lord Jesus Christ save us from the fate of such people, and grant us the portion of the meek and humble!

13.10.0.en: 11 Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase. 12 Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.

13.10.1.en: "Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase." [11]

13.10.2.en: Some see that the wise man is speaking of rich men who built up vast fortunes but did not instill in the lives of their children the spirit of work and striving, so that they rely on what they inherit or on the profit from their inheritance. The children lose the taste of life through slackness and heedlessness, and may even lose the inheritance itself. But he who trains his children to work and strive leaves them an inheritance of a serious, successful and growing life.

13.10.3.en: * If we teach them from the beginning the love of true wisdom, they will have a greater and better wealth than riches bring. If a child learns commerce or receives a high education in a very lucrative profession, all this is counted as nothing compared with the art of renouncing wealth. If you want to make your child rich, teach him this. He is truly rich who does not covet great possessions, nor surround himself with wealth, but asks for nothing!

13.10.4.en: St. John Chrysostom Some see that the discourse here concerns life in the age to come, where the rich whose hearts clung to vain wealth stand in shame, while those who persevere in the spirit of godliness enjoy surpassing glories. The pious man, in the view of St. Augustine, distinguishes between using a thing and enjoying it. He uses what must be used, and enjoys what must be enjoyed, without confusing the two.

13.10.5.en: * To enjoy anything means to cling to it firmly for its own sake. But to use something is to employ what we receive in order to obtain what we need, provided it is fitting for us to need it.

13.10.6.en: * Do not think that silver or gold should be blamed because of the greedy, nor food and wine because of gluttons and drunkards, nor feminine beauty because of adulterers and fornicators. And so in all other matters, especially when you see a physician using fire in a good way while a murderer uses bread with poison in it to carry out his crime.

13.10.7.en: * When Job lost all his wealth and reached the extreme of poverty, he kept himself untroubled, fixed on God, to show that earthly things were of no value in his eyes, but that he was greater than they, and God greater than he. If the men of our days had the same mind, we would not have been persistently forbidden in the New Testament to possess these things in order to reach perfection. For our possessing such things without being attached to them is more praiseworthy than not possessing them at all.

13.11.0.en: St. Augustine "Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life." [12]

13.11.1.en: Here he speaks of dead hope, the hope of the careless man who places his hope in beginning his work, whether spiritual or concerning his job or trade or family, etc., tomorrow, and does not move. For he who does not work and in slackness expects to begin tomorrow, and postpones from day to day, his heart sinks and grows sick, and he loses all vitality. But he who fulfills the desire of his heart and begins to work becomes like one in the Garden of Eden, where he finds the tree of life!

13.11.2.en: But living hope is working hope, where one says with the prodigal son: "I will arise and go to my father... And he arose, and came to his father" (Lk 15:18, 20).

13.12.0.en: 13 Whoso despiseth the word shall be destroyed: but he that feareth the commandment shall be rewarded. 14 The law of the wise is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death. 15 Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard. 16 Every prudent man dealeth with knowledge: but a fool layeth open his folly.

13.12.1.en: "Whoso despiseth the word shall be destroyed: but he that feareth the commandment shall be rewarded." [13]

13.12.2.en: The divine commandment is given to us not to limit our freedom and suppress our will, but to form us by the Spirit of God into a living icon of the Lord Christ, bearing His strong will and enjoying His life working in us. He who makes light of the commandment isolates himself from God, and is shattered. But as for him who fears the commandment of his Father, which issues from God's fatherly love and which we receive in a spirit of sonship, we shall receive the reward of union with Him, and be counted members of God's household, with the right to enter the city of God on high, and we shall not be strangers to God!

13.12.3.en: * The deceitful man, impure in heart, who acquires nothing pure, as Proverbs says: nothing is good for the deceitful (cf. Prov 13:13), is surely counted unworthy to eat the Passover, being a stranger, of a different kind from the saints, and it is said: "No son of a stranger shall eat thereof" (Ex 12:43). So when Judas thought he was keeping the Passover, having devised a plot with deceit against the Savior, he became a stranger to the city on high and to the apostolic company. For the Law commanded that the Passover be eaten with fitting care. But he, as he was eating it, was sifted by Satan, who entered into him.

13.13.0.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic "The law of the wise is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death." [14]

13.13.1.en: What the wise man offers is the divine commandment, the living fountain that waters the soul, so that it does not die of thirst on its journey in the wilderness of this world. The true believer sees in the commandment of the Lord a companion in his exile, like an intimate friend who supports him in facing life. It is a source of consolation to him amid sufferings, and a source of spiritual delight, turning the valley of tears into a joyful, paradisiacal life; therefore he does not practice the commandment under compulsion but with delight.

13.13.2.en: The commandment leads us to streams of living water, and so keeps us from death. The commandment is not deprivation but an enjoyment of the abundant divine gifts that support us during our exile until we reach eternity. For this reason the psalmist says: "I am a stranger in the earth: hide not thy commandments from me" (Ps 119:19). The essential work of the divine commandment is to prepare man for heavenly citizenship; through it he realizes the truth of his position as a stranger and sojourner, and joins the men of faith (Heb 11:13-16). At the same time, his sense of being a stranger moves him to cling to the commandment, that it may support him throughout the time of his exile and lift him up to the heavenly life.

13.13.3.en: * Strangers on the earth need God's commandments to protect them from the works of the flesh and the love of the world.

13.13.4.en: He who follows these commandments, his soul becomes accustomed to them, and the world cannot overcome him.

13.13.5.en: But there are many commandments written in symbols, such as: "And he that is on the housetop, let him not come down to take any thing out of his goods" (Mt 24:17; Mk 13:15; Lk 17:31); "Let the dead bury their dead" (Mt 8:22)... All these are not clear in meaning, likewise the commandments concerning sacrifices, feasts, and clean and unclean animals... Therefore it is fitting for the stranger on the earth to ask God to illumine His commandments for him and not hide them from him, that he may fulfill them and love them and become blameless.

13.13.6.en: Eusebius of Caesarea * My soul longs to keep Your judgments, and to do them with desire, not with weariness and boredom, but with will and constant devotion.

13.14.0.en: Anthimus, Bishop of Jerusalem "Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard." [15]

13.14.1.en: Good understanding and true wisdom give favor to their possessor as they benefit others, but the way of treachery is hard for the treacherous themselves as for others. Treachery or sin makes a man a slave, and its way is full of curses and thorns, and leads to eternal Gehenna.

13.14.2.en: The pious are bound to the word of God, that they may know God's will and fulfill it. They pray zealously, seeking growth in divine wisdom and the enjoyment of understanding as a divine gift, and they persevere in seeking God's grace to support them in practicing the commandment, that they may attain the life of perfection. These experience the blessed life despite the opposition of the wicked to them, and the word of God becomes for them a joyful hymn of praise that carries a special sweetness.

13.14.3.en: * Give me wisdom so that I may test Your law in practice with the attention fitting to it, and thus I may receive from this law the practical exercise.

13.14.4.en: Give me the understanding that pertains to work and contemplation; by this I can "keep it with my whole heart," and draw near to it without hesitation.

13.14.5.en: If wisdom is needed to understand the law, what wisdom must the Lord give the psalmist so that he may discover in it its end and purpose?

13.15.0.en: Origen "Every prudent man dealeth with knowledge: but a fool layeth open his folly." [16]

13.15.1.en: The wise man does not utter a word without knowledge; if he is ignorant of something he keeps silent and admits that he does not know. But the fool, in folly, speaks even of what he does not know.

13.16.0.en: "A wicked messenger falleth into mischief: but a faithful ambassador is health."[17].

13.16.1.en: The wicked messenger, who does not present the person of our Lord Jesus Christ in truth, misleads others, and so harms them and harms or destroys himself. But he who bears witness to the Lord Christ faithfully presents the words of the Lord that give healing.

13.17.0.en: 18 Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured. 19 The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul: but it is abomination to fools to depart from evil. 20 He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be harmed. 21 Evil pursueth sinners: but to the righteous good shall be repaid. 22 A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just. 23 Much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment. 24 He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him seeketh chastening for him.

13.17.1.en: "Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured." [18].

13.17.2.en: He who refuses teaching by one means or another loses everything, even himself, and inward poverty and shame befall him. Then the divine voice is heard: "I will spue thee out of my mouth. Because thou sayest, I am rich" (Rev 3:16-17). But he who bows in humility to learn, even through discipline or reproof, enjoys true knowledge and honor.

13.18.0.en: "The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul: but it is abomination to fools to depart from evil." [19]

13.18.1.en: He who longs for the happy, wise life and declares his longing by practical action, "the desire accomplished or working," his soul enjoys a kind of surpassing sweetness. But he who persists in evil bears the abomination (loathing) of fools.

13.18.2.en: Perhaps by the working desire he means here the believer's acceptance of discipline willingly for the sake of enjoying wisdom, knowledge and truth, and by the abomination of fools he means the fools' rejection of discipline, so that they fail and shame and disgrace come upon them.

13.19.0.en: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be harmed." [20].

13.19.1.en: Wisdom is not sayings recited, nor theories held, but a life lived in all our conduct. Entering into friendships with the wise, with the aim of learning and training in the wise life, supports the believer. Likewise entering into close friendships with the foolish wicked has its effect on a man's life, however careful he is.

13.19.2.en: It is said: "Show me your friends, the books you read and the places you go, and I will know your character!" There is also a common proverb in many languages: "Birds of a feather flock together."

13.19.3.en: * One of the Fathers said: "If a diligent monk lives in a place where there are no other diligent monks, he cannot grow; he can only struggle not to fall behind (that is, not to have his spiritual state worsen). But if a lax monk lives with diligent monks, he grows if he is vigilant, and if not, he at least does not fall behind (that is, go backward)."

13.19.4.en: * Another said: "If you walk with a good companion from your cell to the church, he makes you advance six months, and if you walk with a bad companion from your cell to the church, he sets you back a year."

13.19.5.en: The Garden of the Monks * Do not be a friend of one who loves laughter and prefers to expose people, for he leads you into the habit of relaxation. Do not show cheerfulness in your face to one loose in his conduct, yet guard against hating him. Frown at one who begins to fall upon his brother in front of you... A sweet spring is the conversation of the virtuous. A wise counselor is like a wall of hope. A foolish friend is a store of loss. To watch the mourning women in the house of weeping is better than to see a wise man following a fool.

13.19.6.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian * If you have a friendship with one of the brothers and your thought blames you that your association with him harms you, cut yourself off from him. And I say this, beloved, not that you should hate people, but that you may cut off the causes of vice.

13.19.7.en: St. Mar Ephraim the Syrian * In truth, by the grace of the Lord no obstacle can overthrow your heavenly goal: not desire for wealth, nor your remembering your family, nor inheritance from your relatives, nor familiarity with your brothers, nor love of your households, nor bodily pleasures or luxuries, nor feasts, nor ties of friendship, nor the glory of this age; but you have despised all that, and your very deeds follow the footsteps of the Apostle's saying: "For whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ" (Phil 3:8).

13.19.8.en: Abba Serapion * Do not bind yourself in friendship with any man except your poor brothers; do not hasten toward any man that he may do you good, but hasten to God alone and care for His service, for it is He who gathers you into the bosom of His fatherhood. As for you, beware of familiarity with people, and let all your familiarity be only between you and God. Do not hasten toward any man to enjoy ease in your familiarity with him; do not presume upon his dwelling, and do not stay with him without having received a command to do so, so that you may not be a burden to him. My brother, if you wish to be at rest all your life, and to have your thoughts united with God every hour, beware of familiarity with people. If your brother according to the flesh comes to you and you do not wish to turn him away, take him and hand him over to another brother, where he will find rest in the hearts of the brothers, for they are sincere hearts; but you, remain in your dwelling so that you do not lose the treasures of your wealth.

13.19.9.en: St. Macarius the Great * Strip yourself of evil and put on simplicity; put off the evil eye and put on simplicity and a merciful heart. Do not hate any man; never walk with one of bad conduct, but with one whose conduct is more perfect than yours and who is completing his course. Do not fear the reproach of men; hate everything that harms your soul; do not leave the will of God to do the will of men, that God may be with you.

13.20.0.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great "Evil pursueth sinners: but to the righteous good shall be repaid." [21].

13.20.1.en: Evil comes upon sinners, for it follows their tracks until it surrounds them. They opened the door to it and handed it the steering wheel of their lives, and it leads them to destruction. But as for the righteous, the reward awaits them.

13.20.2.en: Perhaps some are astonished that the wicked flourish in the world, while many sorrows come upon the righteous. But even if the wicked man gains much that seems like success and prosperity, he has lost his inward peace and fears tomorrow. But the righteous believer, in the midst of his many sorrows, God's comforts fill his heart, and his insight is opened to see the glories prepared for him eternally.

13.21.0.en: "A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just." [22]

13.21.1.en: St. John Chrysostom gives us a symbolic interpretation, seeing in the good man here a symbol of the mind, which is often like a father begetting good children, that is, good thoughts, and these in turn beget good thoughts and become fathers of similar deeds.

13.21.2.en: We give a practical example of this: St. Mary, who is righteous and among the righteous, surpassing the heavenly and the earthly beings, has no children or grandchildren according to the flesh. But having carried in her womb the Lover of mankind, the Savior of the world, her heart was enlarged with love toward all mankind, and she became the new Eve, the mother of all living. She has children according to the Spirit, that is, in Christ Jesus. What did she bequeath to her children and her children's children? She enjoyed blessedness, saying: "Behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed" (Lk 1:48). Perhaps the first of her children to inherit this blessedness was the thief on the right, as the Church sings on Good Friday: "Blessed are you, Dismas the thief."

13.22.0.en: "Much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment." [23]

13.22.1.en: The wise man compares a poor man who has a small field which he works, if possible, to the last inch, so that it brings much fruit, with a rich man who has wide fields and in slackness and neglect leaves much of the land unsown!
